Water at soil, not foliage. a 1–2 % neem or potassium bicarbonate spray can slow it; labeled copper or bio-fungicides (Bacillus subtilis, Serenade, etc.) work preventively.

   • Favors: Warm, humid, especially after rain splash.  
   • Action: Same sanitation as above. Copper sprays help only if applied at first sign. Disinfect pruners (10 % bleach or 70 % alcohol) between cuts.

3. Powdery Mildew
   • Appearance: White “flour-dust” patches, often on upper leaf surfaces; spots expand and coalesce.  
   • Favors: Warm, dry days + cool nights (humidity spikes at night).  
   • Action: Remove worst leaves; increase sun exposure; sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, or neem oil sprays every 7–10 days when humidity forecast >60 %. Choose mildew-resistant varieties next season.

4. Sunscald / Ozone damage

I’m sorry your plants are looking under the weather—it can feel discouraging when leaves start to spot or yellow. The good news is that most leaf-spot problems fall into just a few broad categories, and with a little detective work you can usually pin down the cause and take action. Below is a step-by-step way to diagnose what’s happening and some straightforward remedies you can try right away. I’ll assume the spotted plants are your heirloom tomatoes, but the same process works for peppers, eggplants and many common balcony crops.

────────────────────
1. Observe the Spots Closely
────────────────────
Shape, Size & Color
• Pin-point dots (⅛–¼″) with tan or gray centers and dark rims → Septoria leaf spot  
• Larger, brown spots (¼–½″) with faint concentric rings (bulls-eye pattern) → Early blight (Alternaria)  
• Greasy-looking, angular brown/black lesions, sometimes with yellow halos → Bacterial leaf spot  
• Tiny yellow pinpricks that turn bronze or stippled → Spider-mite feeding  
• Irregular tunnels/snakes inside the leaf → Leaf-miner larvae  
• Pale round patches with a crisp, almost bleached look → Sunscald or chemical burn

Where They Start
• Low leaves first, moving upward = most fungal leaf spots  
• Near the top or scattered randomly = sunscald, nutrient splash, or insect pests that move around  

Texture
• Raised bumps, pus-like ooze, or fuzzy mold? That’s a clue to pathogens (fungal or bacterial).  
• Smooth yellowing with no mold = nutrient issue, watering stress, or sunscald.

────────────────────
2. Check Growing Conditions
────────────────────
Air Circulation
• Dense foliage, plants packed tightly, or a balcony with poor airflow traps moisture—prime conditions for fungal spores.

Watering Technique
• Overhead watering splashes spores from soil to leaves; wet foliage that stays damp overnight encourages infection.  
• Inconsistent moisture swings (soak → dry → soak) stress plants and weakens defenses.

Sunlight
• At least 6–8 hours of direct sun is ideal for tomatoes. Less light can slow drying and increase disease pressure.

Soil & Nutrition
• Old potting mix may harbor pathogens.  
• High nitrogen + low calcium can make tissues soft and susceptible.  
• Excess fertilizer salts can “burn” leaf edges, mimicking disease.

────────────────────
3. Quick, Low-Risk First Steps
────────────────────
1. Sanitation  
   • Trim off the worst affected leaves (put them in the trash, not compost).  
   • Sterilize pruners with rubbing alcohol or a 10 % bleach solution between plants.

2. Improve Airflow  
   • Prune a few interior suckers or lower branches.  
   • Space containers so leaves don’t touch.

3. Water Smart  
   • Water at the base early in the day.  
   • Add mulch (straw, coco coir chips, or even clean shredded paper) to reduce soil splash.

4. Strengthen Plants  
   • Top-dress with a balanced organic fertilizer or compost to keep nutrients steady.  
   • Consider a weekly seaweed or fish-emulsion foliar feed (apply to the underside of leaves in the morning when stomata are open).

────────────────────
4. Targeted Treatments If It’s Fungal or Bacterial
────────────────────
• Copper-based fungicide or copper soap: effective on Septoria, early blight, bacterial spot. Follow label; spray in the evening to avoid leaf burn.  
• Sulfur dust or wettable sulfur: preventive for fungal leaf spot (don’t mix with oil sprays or use above 85 °F).  
• Bio-controls: products with Bacillus subtilis (e.g., Serenade) or B. amyloliquefaciens coat leaves and out-compete pathogens; gentle and organic-approved.  
• Neem oil: dual action (fungistatic and insecticidal). Use a 0.5–1 % solution, coat tops/undersides every 7–14 days, evening application to protect pollinators.

Tip: Once leaf-spot diseases show up, sprays mostly slow spread—they don’t “heal” existing lesions. That’s why removing damaged leaves is key.

────────────────────
5. If You Suspect Insects
────────────────────
• Spider mites: Look for fine webbing; leaves feel sand-papery. Blast undersides with water and follow with insecticidal soap or neem.  
• Leaf miners: Squash the tunneling larvae by pinching the squiggles; remove worst leaves.  
• Thrips/whiteflies: Yellow sticky cards help monitor; neem or insecticidal soap every 5–7 days knocks them down.

────────────────────
6. Long-Term Prevention on a Balcony
────────────────────
• Fresh potting mix each year (or solarize/sterilize old mix in black garbage bags under strong sun for 4–6 weeks).  
• Rotate crops even in containers (tomatoes → herbs/lettuce → beans/peas).  
• Choose disease-resistant heirlooms when possible (e.g., ‘Cherokee Purple’ resists Septoria better than ‘Brandywine’).  
• Clean containers with hot soapy water and a 10 % bleach dip before re-planting.  
• Quarantine new plant starts for a week to watch for early symptoms.

────────────────────
7. When You’re Unsure
────────────────────
Take close-up and whole-plant photos in good light and compare them to university extension fact sheets (search “Septoria leaf spot tomato extension” or similar). You can also submit pictures to:

• Your local Cooperative Extension’s “Ask a Master Gardener” service  
• Facebook groups like “Tomato Disease Diagnostics” (large knowledge base, but vet advice carefully)  
• Plant pathology apps (e.g., “PictureThis” or “Plantix”)—use as a first pass, then confirm with reliable sources.

────────────────────
In a Nutshell
────────────────────
• Most balcony tomato leaf spots are either Septoria or early blight.  
• Prune affected foliage, keep leaves dry, improve airflow, and spray preventively with a copper or bio-fungicide.  
• Check for insect pests if spots don’t match typical fungal patterns.  
• Adjust watering and sanitation practices to reduce future outbreaks.

   • For regression: MAE, RMSE, MAPE.  
   • Add a “business metric” (e.g., incremental follower growth).

PHASE 2. COLLECT & CURATE DATA
────────────────────────
A. Core in-platform signals
   • Historical post metadata: timestamp, media type (photo, Reel, carousel), filters, hashtags, caption length.

B. Cross-platform & external signals

   • Calendar context: fashion weeks, holidays, brand drops.

E. Environmental/contextual features
   • Weather API (e.g., temperature in primary follower regions).

As if building a mood board, the richer and more varied your source materials, the more inspired (and generalizable) the final design becomes.

   • Min-max or z-score; categorical one-hot encoding for media types.

   • Use Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, or mutual-information ranking to prune the weakest 20–30 % of features.

A. Baseline (simple, interpretable)

Here's what you could do to figure out if gluten is the issue: 

1. **Elimination diet**: Try avoiding gluten for a few weeks. If your symptoms improve, reintroduce it and see if they return. 

2. **Keep a food diary**: Keep track of everything you eat and note when symptoms occur. Patterns may emerge. 

3. **Try gluten-free products**: Many stores offer gluten-free breads, pastas, and snacks-give them a try! 

4. **Consult a healthcare professional**: A dietitian or doctor can guide you through proper testing and diagnosis, like a celiac diseases test or other screenings. 

If gluten does turn out to be a problem, no worries! There are tons of delicious gluten-free recipes to keep your culinary adventures exciting.

* **Digital Gifts**: Offer digital gifts like subscriptions to eco-friendly magazines, online courses related to sustainability, or memberships to virtual experiences such as wine tastings or cooking classes.
* **Sustainable Office Supplies**: Send high-quality, sustainable office supplies like notebooks made from recycled paper, bamboo pens, or solar-powered gadgets. These are practical and align with eco-friendly values.
* **Charitable Donations**: Make a donation to a UK-based environmental charity or a cause that your partner supports. This not only reflects your commitment to sustainability but also shows thoughtfulness and consideration.
* **Plant-Based Gifts**: Consider sending a plant or a tree planting kit. Plants can brighten up an office space and contribute to a healthier environment. Alternatively, you can donate to a tree-planting initiative in their name.
* **Experience Gifts**: Offer experiences that can be enjoyed locally, such as a voucher for a sustainable restaurant, a day at an eco-friendly spa, or tickets to a green event or workshop.

By choosing gifts that align with your partner's values and interests, you can strengthen your business relationship while navigating the post-Brexit landscape effectively.

Billy Pilgrim, a mild, often passive man, experiences his life out of chronological order. One moment he is a scrawny infantryman captured by the Germans; the next, he is an older husband at a 1960s optometrists’ convention; then he is naked in a glass dome on the planet Tralfamadore, observed by aliens who perceive all of time simultaneously. The book loops repeatedly through these periods, always circling back to the Allied bombing of Dresden in February 1945. • The absurdity and inevitability of death  
• The randomness of survival during war  
• Free will vs. determinism (Tralfamadorian time)  
• Trauma, memory, and nonlinear recollection

• Postmodern playfulness: author intrusions, fragmented structure.

2\. **Use Call and Response**: This technique involves singing a phrase and having the choir repeat it back to you. This can help them get comfortable with the melody before adding harmonies.

3\. **Teach by Rote**: Since your choir members don't read music, you'll need to teach the harmonies by ear. You can do this by singing the harmony part yourself and having the choir repeat it back to you.

4\. **Recorded Parts**: Consider providing recordings of each part for choir members to practice with at home. This can help them become more familiar with their parts and build confidence.

5\. **Visual Aids**: Use visual aids to help them understand the structure of the song. This could be a simple diagram showing which parts sing when, or color-coded lyrics.

6\. **Practice in Sections**: Start by practicing the harmonies in small groups before bringing everyone together. This can help each section feel more confident with their part.

7\. **Patience and Encouragement**: Remember, learning to sing in harmony can be challenging, especially for those who don't read music. Be patient, offer plenty of encouragement, and celebrate small victories along the way.

Quantum teleportation is more than a headline-grabbing “Star Trek–style” trick: it is a workhorse protocol for moving fragile quantum information (qubit states) from one physical location to another without physically transferring the qubit itself. Because Quantum AI (QAI) systems ultimately need to shuttle qubit states between chips, racks, data centres or edge devices, teleportation is poised to become as fundamental to QAI networking as TCP/IP is to classical cloud AI.

Below is a concise primer on quantum teleportation, followed by the concrete ways it can reshape data transfer and communication in QAI and the practical hurdles that still have to be solved.

────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Quantum teleportation in a nutshell
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Minimum ingredients  
  – An entangled Bell pair |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 shared between “Alice” (sender) and “Bob” (receiver).  
  – A Bell-state measurement on Alice’s side that projects her half of the pair plus the unknown qubit |ψ⟩ into one of four Bell states.  
  – Two classical bits sent from Alice to Bob telling him which corrective Pauli (I, X, Z, or XZ) to apply.  

• What is (and isn’t) achieved  
  – The full quantum state |ψ⟩ is re-created on Bob’s side, while the original is destroyed (no-cloning respected).  
  – No faster-than-light signalling: the classical two-bit message constrains the speed to at most c.  
  – Fidelity is limited by the quality of the shared entanglement and the measurement apparatus.

────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Why QAI systems care
────────────────────────────────────────────
A. Distributed quantum-AI “data centres”  
   • Scaling via entanglement-swapped networks: Large-scale QAI workloads may need thousands-to-millions of logical qubits, which will not fit on one cryostat or photonic chip in the foreseeable future. Teleportation lets geographically separated quantum-processing units (QPUs) stitch themselves into a single logical computer by swapping/teleporting states through repeaters.  
   • Analogy: What MPI and RDMA do for GPU clusters, teleportation plus entanglement-assisted routing could do for QPU clusters.

B. Teleportation-based gates for fault-tolerant QAI circuits  
   • “Gate teleportation” is already central to error-corrected quantum computing: non-Clifford gates (e.g., the T-gate) are executed by preparing special “magic states” and teleporting them into the data block. Because essentially every serious QML algorithm used in QAI (quantum GANs, variational classifiers, QSVMs, etc.) becomes gate-teleportation heavy once you add error correction, improvements in teleportation fidelity/time map directly onto QAI throughput.

C. Overcoming limited chip connectivity  
   • In superconducting and trapped-ion processors, only neighbouring qubits interact natively. Teleportation lets you “beam” a logical qubit to a distant register, bypassing SWAP ladders that would otherwise add depth and decoherence to QAI circuits.

D. Secure, privacy-preserving quantum machine learning  
   • Blind QML: A client teleports encrypted (one-time-padded) quantum data to a remote QAI server. Because the raw state never exists at the server prior to the Pauli corrections, the provider learns nothing.  
   • Federated quantum learning: Edge quantum sensors (e.g., NV-centre magnetometers) can teleport model updates to a central learner while keeping data localized.

E. Real-time streaming from quantum sensors  
   • Applications such as quantum lidar or satellite-borne entangled-photon imagers could teleport sensed qubits to ground-based QAI analyzers, avoiding decoherence over the entire path.

────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Expected benefits
────────────────────────────────────────────
• Latency reduction: With good repeater chains, long-haul links can approach the speed-of-light classical limit without extra quantum routing overhead.  
• Fidelity preservation: Teleportation can shift qubits onto fresh, less-noisy physical carriers, effectively acting as an “information swap-out” that resets error budgets.  
• Modularity: Hardware manufacturers can specialise—one node for memory, one for processing—knowing that teleportation will glue the system together.  
• Security “for free”: Eavesdropping breaks entanglement correlations, giving automatic intrusion detection.

────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Key technical challenges
────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Entanglement distribution rate  
   – Current on-demand entanglement generation is kHz–MHz, whereas petahertz-level rates would be ideal for cloud-scale QAI.

2. Quantum repeaters and memories  
   – Needed for long-distance (>100 km) links. High-coherence memories (ms–s) plus purification protocols are still experimental.

3. Fidelity vs. throughput trade-off  
   – Purifying entanglement improves fidelity but costs multiple Bell pairs per final high-quality pair, throttling bandwidth for QAI workloads.

4. Chip-level integration  
   – Compact, cryo-compatible photonic interfaces for superconducting processors or efficient microwave-to-optic transducers remain engineering bottlenecks.

5. Classical-quantum orchestration  
   – Teleportation is useless without nanosecond-timing classical control (to send correction bits) that can keep pace with QAI clock cycles.

────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Roadmap snapshot
────────────────────────────────────────────
Near-term (1-3 yrs)  
• In-fridge teleportation between separate chips sharing a cryostat; proof-of-concept distributed QNN training across two racks.

Mid-term (3-7 yrs)

Long-term (7–15 yrs)  
• “Quantum internet” enabling wide-area QAI cloud services where qubits, not just classical parameters, are the unit of data exchange.  
• Edge-to-cloud teleportation pipelines powering secure, on-device quantum-enhanced sensing and AI inference.

────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Bottom line
────────────────────────────────────────────
Quantum teleportation is less about science-fiction transport and more about reliable, high-fidelity relocation of quantum information—the lifeblood of any Quantum AI workflow. Its eventual maturation will:

• determine how we scale QAI beyond the capacity of single devices,  
• underpin fault-tolerant logic needed for serious QML algorithms, and  
• enable fundamentally new paradigms of secure, distributed and privacy-preserving quantum-AI computation.

In short, teleportation will be to Quantum AI networks what optical fiber became to the classical internet: the invisible but indispensable backbone that makes everything else possible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

• Bob uses them to apply one of four Pauli corrections (I, X, Z, XZ).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Why “moving” qubits matters for Quantum AI
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Classical deep-learning speedups arose from three hardware ideas: GPUs (parallel compute), fast memory hierarchies, and high-bandwidth interconnects (NVLink, Infiniband).  An analogous story is emerging for Quantum AI:

• Compute layer = superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, or neutral-atom qubits that execute parameterized circuits, variational algorithms, etc.  
• Memory layer = quantum memories or registers that store intermediate quantum states.  
• Interconnect layer = teleportation and entanglement distribution networks.

────────────────────────────────────────

────────────────────────────────────────
Why gels or powders instead of the liquid drops sold in grocery stores?
•  Gels (e.g., AmeriColor, Chefmaster) and powders are highly concentrated.

•  They are shelf-stable, inexpensive, and allergen-free (always check the label).

2.  Add 1–2 tiny drops of gel color (or a toothpick’s worth for powders).

• Freeze-dried blueberry or blackberry powder (½ tsp powder per ½ cup sugar)

Step 1: Gather Ingredients

- 1 cup all-purpose flour
- 1 cup cherries, pitted and halved
- 1 small onion, finely chopped
- 1 clove garlic, minced
- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- 1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves
- 1 teaspoon fresh rosemary, finely chopped
- 1/2 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon black pepper
- 1/2 cup red wine
- 1/2 cup vegetable broth
- 1 tablespoon honey
- 1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar
- 1 tablespoon unsalted butter
- 1/4 cup crumbled feta cheese (optional)

Step 2: Prepare the Cherries

- In a small bowl, combine the pitted and halved cherries with 1 tablespoon of honey. Set aside.

Step 3: Cook the Onion and Garlic

- Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat.
- Add the chopped onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes.
- Add the minced garlic and cook for another minute.

Step 4: Add the Flour

- Sprinkle the all-purpose flour over the onion and garlic mixture.
- Stir well to combine and cook for 2-3 minutes, until the flour is lightly browned.

Step 5: Add Wine, Broth, and Herbs

- Pour in the red wine and vegetable broth, stirring constantly to avoid lumps.
- Add the fresh thyme leaves, chopped rosemary, salt, and black pepper.
- Bring the mixture to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes, until the sauce has thickened.

Step 6: Add Cherries and Balsamic Vinegar

- Stir in the honey-coated cherries and balsamic vinegar.
- Cook for another 5 minutes, until the cherries are softened and the sauce has reduced slightly.

Step 7: Finish with Butter and Feta

- Remove the skillet from the heat and stir in the unsalted butter until melted.
- Taste and adjust the seasoning if necessary.
- If desired, sprinkle crumbled feta cheese over the top before serving.

Step 8: Serve and Enjoy

- This cherry and flour-based savory dish can be served as a side or main course, accompanied by rice, pasta, or crusty bread. Enjoy the unique combination of sweet cherries and savory herbs in this innovative recipe!

Title: The Art of Haiku – One-Day Creative Writing Workshop  
Date/Time: Saturday, 8:00 a.m. – 5:00 p.m.

Objective  
• Give participants a working knowledge of haiku history, form, and aesthetics.  
• Explore imagery, seasonal reference, juxtaposition, and “cutting” techniques that create resonance in as few words as possible.  
• Provide extensive guided practice, feedback, and revision so each writer leaves with several polished poems and one display-ready favorite.  
• Foster a shared experience of bringing poetry into a public space through an outdoor haiku installation.

Materials  
• Sample packets of classical & contemporary haiku  
• Syllable-count cheat sheets and seasonal word (kigo) lists  
• Clipboards or notebooks, pens/pencils  
• Colored cardstock strips (2" × 8") and twine/ribbon for tree display  
• Clothespins or paper clips  
• Portable timer or bell  
• Whiteboard/markers

Schedule

8:00 – 8:30   Introduction & Overview  
• Welcome, goals, and logistics  
• Quick historical timeline: hokku to modern haiku  
• Core formal elements: 3 lines, 17-syllable guideline, seasonal reference, kireji/cutting word

8:30 – 9:00   Group Discussion: What Makes a Memorable Haiku?  
• Read 4–5 classics aloud  
• Identify sensory details, implied narrative, and emotional turn

9:00 – 9:45   Writing Exercise #1: “First Impressions”  
• Silent garden walk (or slide images if indoors) to note sensory impressions  
• Draft two haiku using simple 5-7-5 scaffolding

9:45 – 10:00  Break

10:00 – 10:30  Peer Review Round 1  
• Small-group reading  
• Compliment-question-suggest format focused on clarity & imagery

10:30 – 12:00  Extended Workshop: Advanced Techniques  
• Juxtaposition & internal “cut”  
• Negative space and minimalism  
• Seasonality beyond nature: social or emotional seasons  
• Brief mini-lectures interwoven with 5-minute micro-writes and share-backs

12:00 – 1:00  Lunch & Informal Discussion  
• Eat together while exploring haiku’s place in contemporary literature, social media, and visual art  
• Optional open-mic for favorite poets or spontaneous drafts

1:00 – 1:30  Writing Exercise #2: Apply an Advanced Technique  
• Choose one focus (juxtaposition, negative space, unconventional kigo) and craft two new haiku

1:30 – 2:15  Peer Review & Revision Round 2  
• Line-by-line tightening  
• Test reading aloud for rhythm and breath

2:15 – 2:30  Break

2:30 – 3:15  Selection & Fine-Tuning for Display  
• Revisit all drafts, choose one “signature” haiku  
• Copy neatly onto colored cardstock; punch hole & attach twine

3:15 – 4:15  Garden Haiku Installation  
• Move outside; affix poems to the designated tree  
• Stroll, read, photograph, and quietly reflect on others’ work

4:15 – 4:45  Reflection Circle  
• Share discoveries about process, surprises, and next steps  
• Quick verbal feedback on workshop structure

4:45 – 5:00  Closing Remarks  
• Collect unused materials, distribute resource list & further reading  
• Thank-you and departure

──────────────────────────────────────────

──────────────────────────────────────────
00:50-01:20  | Practical Applications Skills Lab (30 min)
──────────────────────────────────────────

————————————————————
1. LORE & VISUAL / AUDIO FLAIR
————————————————————
Super-weapon name (pick one or mix):
• Sol-Lens Strike System (S.L.S.S.)  
• “Archangel” Orbital Concussion Array  
• Orbital Photonic Concussion Cannon (OPCC)

1) A bank of solar-powered Fresnel lenses or phased plasma mirrors held in GEO.  
2) When fired, they focus sunlight (plus a small antimatter “seed” charge if you want a sci-fi nod) onto a ground point.  
3) Energy deposition creates a micro-plasma bubble→atmospheric overpressure→detonation.  
4) Shock front collapses inward like a spherical-wave, then snaps outward in a flat disc—exactly the “ring” visual of Jango Fett’s seismic charge and an accompanying bass-shock “bwong” one frame after the flash.  
5) Light output peaks at ~10^17 lumens at origin; bright enough that the flash saturates every skybox no matter the camera zoom.  In lore the burst is “technically visible from Mars or even Venus given line-of-sight,” satisfying your Olympus-Mons requirement.

Speed of sound in space issue: because it’s a game you can cheat—render the flash, hold silence for ≈1.5 s, then tack on the detonation “snap” so players get the same eerie moment of dread the movie scene has.

————————————————————
2. GAMEPLAY STATS & BALANCE
————————————————————
Baseline assumptions
• Standard land super-weapon in similar RTS titles does 100–150 % of a main-base HP bar in a 1.5-tile radius, cooldown 6–7 min.  
• You plan 5-min recharge.  Make the absolute footprint smaller or its prep time longer to compensate.

Suggested numbers
Damage: 90 % of a full HQ / command center HP pool at epicenter, linear falloff to 30 % at edge of radius.  
Radius: 2.5 building tiles (roughly half a normal nuke).  
Wind-up: 15-s “align mirrors” warning laser column visible to enemy (gives counter-play).  
Recharge: 5:00 real-time.  
Cost: ~1.4× the mineral / currency cost of the conventional nuke silo, because the strike is more precise and reloads quicker.

Why these values work
• Lower raw damage than nuke + smaller AoE keeps it from wiping an entire base in one go.  
• Precision & quick reload make it a surgical sledgehammer: great vs. clustered power plants, super-weapons or airfields.  
• The loud flash + distinct ring notifies every player instantly—good for spectacle & clarity.

————————————————————
3. COUNTERPLAY / TECH TREE TIE-INS
————————————————————
• Satellite-Jam Field: Advanced radar-jam generator that forces the Sol-Lens to take 50 % longer to “lock,” buying defenders extra evac time.  
• Mirror-Scramble Drones (mid-tech air unit): Circles the target area, causing strike to mis-focus and do only 40 % damage.  
• Hardened Bunkers / Blast Mesh upgrade: Reduces photonic strike damage to infantry inside by 60 %.

————————————————————
4. PERFORMANCE & ENGINE TIPS
————————————————————
• Flash: single full-screen additive white sprite w/ exponential fade (<0.5 s) + bloom, then HDR lens-flare bloom for 2 s.  
• Shock ring: project a torus mesh scaled outward over 1.2 s; z-write off, additive shader, noise dissolve.  
• Audio: multi-layer sample—(1) low-passed explosion for the “snap,” (2) sub-100 Hz rumbler synced to camera shake, (3) mid-band crackle tail.  
• Network sync: transmit just target coords + seed so clients build visuals locally, avoiding >1 kB payload.

————————————————————
5. LORE BLURB (for tool-tips or cut-scene VO)
————————————————————
“Born of a UN black-budget solar-engineering project, the Sol-Lens Strike System array stores zero warheads on site—just sunlight and nerve.  When the mirrors align, a plasma bloom nine times hotter than the photosphere detonates at ground zero.  The flash is so brilliant that Mars surveyors have logged it.  Survivors describe the sound as reality itself ‘snapping.’  Doctrine limits consecutive deployments to one every five minutes to prevent orbital cooling-coil burnout—mercifully for those below.”

6. OPTIONAL VARIANTS FOR OTHER FACTIONS

• Seismic Resonator (underground shock that ignores walls but hurts only structures).
